**Acts 1**

*The former treatise have I made, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began both to do and teach,*

*2 Until the day in which he was taken up, after that he through the Holy Ghost had given commandments unto the apostles whom he had chosen:*

*3 To whom also he shewed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs, being seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God:*

*4 And, being assembled together with them, commanded them that they should not depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which, saith he, ye have heard of me.*

*5 For John truly baptized with water; but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence.*

*6 When they therefore were come together, they asked of him, saying, Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?*

*7 And he said unto them, It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power.*

*8 But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.*

*9 And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight.*

*10 And while they looked stedfastly toward heaven as he went up, behold, two men stood by them in white apparel;*

*11 Which also said, Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven.*

*12 Then returned they unto Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is from Jerusalem a sabbath day's journey.*

*13 And when they were come in, they went up into an upper room, where abode both Peter, and James, and John, and Andrew, Philip, and Thomas, Bartholomew, and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon Zelotes, and Judas the brother of James.*

*14 These all continued with one accord in prayer and supplication, with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brethren.*

*15 And in those days Peter stood up in the midst of the disciples, and said, (the number of names together were about an hundred and twenty,)*

*16 Men and brethren, this scripture must needs have been fulfilled, which the Holy Ghost by the mouth of David spake before concerning Judas, which was guide to them that took Jesus.*

*17 For he was numbered with us, and had obtained part of this ministry.*

*18 Now this man purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out.*

*19 And it was known unto all the dwellers at Jerusalem; insomuch as that field is called in their proper tongue, Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood.*

*20 For it is written in the book of Psalms, Let his habitation be desolate, and let no man dwell therein: and his bishoprick let another take.*

*21 Wherefore of these men which have companied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us,*

*22 Beginning from the baptism of John, unto that same day that he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection.*

*23 And they appointed two, Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias.*

*24 And they prayed, and said, Thou, Lord, which knowest the hearts of all men, shew whether of these two thou hast chosen,*

*25 That he may take part of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas by transgression fell, that he might go to his own place.*

*26 And they gave forth their lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.*

The book of Acts, composed by Luke, is a continuation of his account of the gospel, written to a man named Theophilus.

We see Acts reflect the familiar opening to Theophilus in **Luke 1:1-4**
*Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us, Even as they delivered them unto us, which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word; It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus, That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.*

The risen Jesus instructs his disciples to remain in Jerusalem until the Holy Ghost comes, giving gifts unto them for their ministry. Luke recounts again the great commission given by Jesus to them (Luke 24), to spread the good news that all might believe, *both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.*

We see in Luke's account that this is the final command of Christ, and that He then ascended into the heavens in His glory.

Two angels of the Lord give comfort to them, and prophecy of the second coming. That Jesus will return in the same manner He left, coming in the clouds.

The remaining 11 apostles and another 100 or so staying in a great room in Jerusalem, agree with Peter that they must select a 12th from those disciples who were with the ministry from the beginning. From John the Baptist on.

Peter tells the fate of Judas, who betrayed Christ. That in his suicide by hanging, his body fell and split wide open, and even the non-believer Jews view the plot he'd died on as cursed.

Peter continues the manner of preaching of Jesus, calling upon the scriptures. Having been saved and his spirit quickened by that faith, Peter sees the prophecy and fulfilment of God's word.

Joseph/Barsabas Justus and Matthias. And praying and voting they cast lots and elect Matthias.

Old business taken care of, new orders of business about to begin.

Fun Fact regarding Pentecost:

The High Holy day, called the Festival of Weeks or "Shavuot," is 7 weeks following the second day of Passover (feast of unleavened bread). In Greek, Pentecost, meaning 50 days following Passover itself.

 Passover commemorates God freeing the Israelites from Egypt, Pentecost, the Feast of Weeks celebrates the day of the giving of the law by Moses and commitment of the people to agree to God's covenant and be His people, detailed in **Exodus 34.**

In the midst of chapter 34, almost as an afterthought, we find verse 22:
*And thou shalt observe the feast of weeks, of the firstfruits of wheat harvest, and the feast of ingathering at the year's end.*

As we know, at Pentecost in Acts, the Apostles and disciples receive gifts of the Holy Ghost, and begin preaching to the multitudes gathered in Jerusalem for the feast, and bring 3000 thousand to salvation.

Literally the first fruits of the harvest.

What an amazing God we have. What a blessing His word is.

Acts chapter 2 picks up now, 10 days after Jesus' ascension, the 120 disciples and Apostles gathered in church, waiting in Jerusalem as Jesus had instructed. As they waited, suddenly the great room they were in was filled with a rushing wind and flames of fire, filling those assembled with the Holy Ghost.

The traditional teaching of this chapter says that this is the first time the Holy Ghost is indwelling in believers, quickening their spirit the same way saved Christians experience today, calling upon the name of the Lord. It's often preached as "until Pentecost, no one had the indwelling of the Holy Ghost." The Bible says in the OT believers who called upon the name of the Lord and were saved by faith did not have the Holy Ghost permanently within them, but were often described as being filled with Him at times to do great feats, prophesy and preach, or be used in some way to the glory of God. I believe this is what's happening here, because in John 20:22 (which we just read), where risen Christ appears to them on Easter Sunday, the scripture says:

*And when he had said this, he breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost.*

I believe this was when the Holy Ghost, the comforter and 3rd person of the triune Godhead, first indwelled in those who are quickened by faith, in God's grace.

I could be wrong but that's how it reads to me, otherwise John is contradicting Acts, impossible. Given the context of what happens next, I think my interpretation is correct.

Now, on the primary holy day of the feast of Pentecost, believing, practicing Jews from all over the world were required to make pilgrimage to Jerusalem and the temple for the feast of first fruits of the harvest, and the blood free will sacrifices of purification (Exodus 23:16, 34:22, Leviticus 23:16, Numbers 28:26).

The Bible says that these Jews came from every nation, and lists many of the nations in example. And as the 120, filled with the Spirit come out to the crowd this gathered, they begin to preach the Gospel to all, in their own languages. This miracle of God is astounding, as these faithful God-fearing people hear the good news of Jesus Christ in their native tongue.

Not the satanic gibberish of the Charismatics and so-called Pentecostals, but clear understandable language of those assembled there.

Not the mistaken doctrine that the disciples spoke Hebrew or Aramaic or Greek, and those assembled heard it in their own languages, but if speaking to a Mede or Libyan or whatever land the pilgrims were from, they were able to communicate the Gospel to them. How do we know this? By the reaction of the Jews from Jerusalem, who mocked what they heard as unintelligible chatter as their being drunken.

This is when Peter gives a blistering sermon addressed specifically to those mocking, and an indictment of the Jews of Judea.

Peter says obviously they aren't drunken, being only 9 in the morning, but that it's fulfilled prophecy. He then quotes Joel regarding how in the last days the sons and daughters will prophesy, and uses that verse to then lead them the further prophecy of Joel of the second coming of Christ.

Peter is not simply defending their speaking in tongues, but like Jesus did repeatedly in His ministry, Peter is using scripture they should be familiar with to bring them the Gospel. He quotes Joel 3's warning of what the day of the Lord will look like, and indicating to the crowd that it is all coming true. Warning them that if they are seeing sons and daughters with signs and wonders, preaching the word, maybe they should take heed of what the rest of scripture says. That "*Whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved."*

This is the Gospel.

He continues, making clear precisely who Jesus is, what He did, that He did it among them as they well know, and that despite their knowledge they killed Christ. Peter lays the blame for this squarely on the Jews in Jerusalem.

Continuing the Gospel, Peter tells them of the resurrection, Jesus overcoming death, and points to Psalm 16 where David writing in the Spirit, gives prophecy of Jesus. Peter reminds them that David wasn't speaking of himself as his body was buried in the sepulchre. That David was speaking of Christ to come, which the disciples were testifying they had seen risen, first hand.

Peter explains that having fulfilled God's promise, they had received the Holy Ghost, and the masses witness of this miracle of the tongues is evidence that all of this is true.

*Therefore let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made the same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ.*

Hearing the Gospel and the truth of the good news and changing their minds, accepting the truth, understanding the role they played in killing the Son of God, they believed. And they asked "what shall we do?"

Peter replies "*repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.*"

Note the order of things. Peter gives them the Gospel. They ask what they now must do. Peter tells them repent, or change their mind. Not "of sin" but of what they, *in ignorance* and *unbelief* did, participating in His death. That they believe. Then they should be baptized in Jesus' name. Proving their belief. That they will have remission of sins and the gift of the Holy Ghost from that change of mind, of their repentance to believing on Him.

This statement confuses the unsaved as much as anything else in the Bible. They isolate it, out of context to teach repent of sins heresy and the false understanding that baptism is what gives us remission of sins, despite multiple examples throughout scripture that it is the belief and calling upon the name of the Lord that gives us salvation. That remission of sins comes from Christ Jesus, not of the works or rites we do.

Stripped of all context, including who Peter is speaking to, what they did, the unbelief they shared and why they must repent from it, to accept Jesus as the Christ, many are led astray.

Peter and the other 120 continue soul winning the crowd, exhorting them to *save themselves from this untoward generation*.

They that received the good news and believed were then baptized. (Again note the order of operations).

And so 120 saved 3,000. What's wonderful about this is those souls were from all nations on earth, and so God having created this feast of the first fruits, created the way for the news of the Gospel to be spread to every corner of the world, 1,300yrs before this fateful day.

Acts 3 is a short chapter detailing the healing of the lame man at the Beautiful Gate of the temple. Peter, with John, heals the man in Jesus Christ's name, who begins leaping with joy into the temple, the crowd amazed. Luke, being a physician wants us to know his malformed ankle bones are set right by the power of God.

Peter again preaches to the Jews, their guilt in the crucifixion of Jesus, that the prophets all told them was coming, the Christ who the patriarchs had faith in and were justified as that faith was counted on them for righteousness.

Peter again indicts them for their murder of the Son of God and even throws in a jab at their choosing Barabbas.

To this crime and their lack of belief in Jesus as He ministered to them, Peter says to repent and be converted, turn from that disbelief and be changed into a saved child of God. Believe them that their sins may be blotted out.

Peter's appeal to the prophets, more direct that Jesus' deliberate dark sayings had been, is the theme taken up by Paul in his Epistles as well. It is important to understand that the whole Bible, Old Testament and New, is about Jesus Christ. And that the faith that saves and imputes righteousness on believers is the same, since the beginning. Faith in the lamb slain at the foundation of the world.

Chapter 4 picks up immediately after 3, and the healing of the lame man at the Temple gate. The Jews are angry again, this time the Sadducees who were a sect that denied Heaven or the Resurrection.

It's important to understand that they're denial of the literal body Resurrection of the righteous was their doctrine that predated Jesus Christ's coming. There are many who foolishly will say that the OT didn't teach on Jesus or a resurrection in the last day, that it was a concept invented later, yet there being a prominent sect opposed to the teaching established in the temple pretty much destroys that nonsense.

The Sadducees are very much like today's reformed Jew, that carry the trappings as ceremony, but teach a vague, satanic deism absent the glory and power of God. Much of the conflict between factions of modern Jews reflects the split between the Sadducees and Pharisees, who claim a belief in God and the afterlife, but again deny His power, trusting their own. Think the Globohomo diaspora Jews vs the Orthodox, Chabad Lubavitch Zionist Jews.

Both despise Christ and Christians.

*30 And when he had thus spoken, the king rose up, and the governor, and Bernice, and they that sat with them:*

*31 And when they were gone aside, they talked between themselves, saying, This man doeth nothing worthy of death or of bonds.*

*32 Then said Agrippa unto Festus, This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Caesar.*

Having been called before the king, Agrippa, Paul is given the opportunity to speak freely in his defense.

Bound and chained before them, Paul explains himself.

He again gives his testimonial, of how he came from the Pharisees with zeal against the believers of Christ, to his roadside visitation by Jesus, and his ministry to bring the truth, preached by all the prophets before then, that Christ must come and the resurrection that follows.

Paul says he showed the truth of the Gospel *first unto them of Damascus, and at Jerusalem, and throughout all the coasts of Judaea, and then to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, and do works meet for repentance. For these causes the Jews caught me in the temple, and went about to kill me.*

We see Biblical repentance in regards to salvation is turning from what ever is being believed in regards to God's word, and turning towards God for salvation. That, as we have seen again and again, it's always used in this fashion. That the "...of sin," or whatever isn't mentioned. It is turning your trust from false beliefs, your own works, false gods and idols, and towards God. And once saved doing works suitable and proper for such a turning.

This, Paul says is why the Jews want him dead, as the book of Acts has shown us again and again. This message of hope and good news of the resurrection, and their role in killing Christ, and their resentment at losing the inheritance to the Gentiles has always been why the Jew persecutest God's people.

Even today, making Gentiles unworthy of God's inheritance is their goal, and the subversive nature of the Jew is dedicated to this cause, and preventing those of us who have obtained our portion of the kingdom of God from giving others the same adoption of faith.

Festus yelling out, "*Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad*" is a familiar tactic of those proud in their own conceits when confronted with the truth of the word. We see this mockery and derision often, when we speak out for the Lord. Especially when it's done confidently and with knowledge of the scriptures. Left with having to either acknowledge the truth or save face and defend the status they hold in pride, most choose to be scornful.

And Agrippa, who history paints as a hedonist, possibly engaged in incest with his sister Bernice (who is present for this), laughingly says Paul has almost convinced him to be a Christian.

I believe him to be reprobate, based on this mocking response. One quality of the reprobate mind according to Romans 1, is that *knowing the truth*, they reject it. I find this true in my own experience with them. Most reprobates when pushed understand the basics of salvation and Christ. Often better than some who call themselves Christian but who are caught up in damnable heresy. It's a head knowledge coupled with a hardness of heart and stiffness of neck, that brought them to be twice-dead, conscience seared.

Paul expresses the fervent hope that all who hear him come to saving faith, that the hearers be as he is, absent his current bonds, and with that they dismiss him. Agrippa then says that while Paul hasn't done anything to be held, his appeal unto Caesar has sealed his fate. Paul is destined for Rome.

It is in the hands of Christians, Bible believing, born again sons of God, to turn away from their wicked ways, their indulgence in the world, in sin, in the subversive and perverse things we are tempted with, and turn towards God the Father, in Jesus' name.

All other methods of delaying the wrath that America deserves are vanity. We cannot vote our way out. We cannot shoot our way out. We cannot riot and murder and exact our own vengeance, and expect any relief.

Paul's visitation by a messenger of God, promise to save the crew and passengers. The fasting of the believers among them, the breaking of bread and the casting off of the wheat to the sea. The final chapter of Acts. Thank God for His word.

Luke writes of their being waylaid on the island they castaway on, *Melita* (Malta), and its barbarian population led by a man named Publius. The Maltese are hospitable to the crew, centurions and prisoners.

We are told that after gathering a bundle of sticks (ahem), and burning them in the fire, a venomous snake bites Paul in the hand, causing the natives to assume he be a murderer that having escaped shipwreck was now being taken out by snake.

However, as Jesus said if those apostles given the gifts of the Holy Ghost in Mark 16:18 “*They shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them; they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover*.”

And thus, Paul shakes the snake off into the fire and is fine. Further, he heals Publius' father of dysentery, and goes on to heal many of the Maltese people during their stay, lasting 3 months. They leave with a ship that had wintered in port, honored by the chief and his people, and so, as Paul writes in Romans 1:14, *“I am debtor both to the Greeks, and to the Barbarians.*"

There are snake handling sects claiming they are "apostles," and that venom cannot hurt them, who speak gibberish and call it 'speaking in tongues," and engage in other nonsense, LARPing at the things of God, more African voodoo than Christian.

There is no record in the Bible of Publius' conversion or of any preaching of the word, or the Gospel having any effect on the people there. Generally there are mentions of 'some believed,' or a summation of Paul giving the good news of Christ and it is hard to imagine he didn't, given his zeal and the healings we are told he performed, but there's no indication either way. That hasn't stopped the RCC from declaring Publius a saint and naming him a bishop, posthumously.

So, finally coming to Italy and heading to Rome, they meet brothers in Christ, and we are told this was an encouragement to Paul. And arriving in Rome, Paul is placed under house arrest. Tradition holds that Paul was chained to his guard, 24 hours a day, as was Roman custom in such cases. Roman guards typically restrained prisoners with chains. The prisoner’s right wrist was usually chained to the guard’s left wrist. This kept the guard’s right hand free. Paul referred to his chains, bonds, and imprisonment in most of the epistles he wrote during his house arrest in Rome..(Eph 3:1; 4:1; 6:20; Php 1:7, 13, 14, 17; Col 4:3, 18; Phm 1, 9, 10, 13)

Paul calls on the Jews of Rome, and tells them of his plight and treatment by the Jews of Asia, in Jerusalem and leading to his being in Rome to appeal to Nero. He preaches to them from scripture, proving all things about Jesus being the Christ. And, as we have seen more than once, while many believed, most had stiff necks and hardened hearts. Here, quoting **Isaiah 6:8-10** in the same way Jesus does in **Matthew 13:15**, we see them unable to understand the Gospel and believe, by their own choosing.

*But the salvation of God is sent unto the Gentiles, and they will hear it.* Jews, so-called, to this day resent and hate the Gentile for this.

We are told Paul remained in bonds in his own hired house for 2 full years, preaching of Jesus. We know of the epistles he wrote while under bonds. We know he must have reached some of Caesar's household as he says in his letter to the **Philippians, 4:22**, "*All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household."*

We know Nero hadn't quite gone full Reprobate by this time, and we have no evidence Paul went before him or just simply was released. Tradition has it that he was freed after the two years, and that his mission then took him to Spain, preaching the word. Some later historians claim he was arrested again and martyred in Rome by beheading. Others have said the evidence is flimsy, and he likely died of old age while still evangelizing. We simply don't know. But the important thing to Paul was always Jesus, spreading the faith in Him, first to the Jew and then the Greek. Amen.

Before beginning another book of the Bible, I just want to reflect back on what we have seen consistently: In John, the only book written explicitly to the unsaved that they may believe and receive eternal life, where in every chapter, Jesus teaches that it is by faith alone we are saved. In Acts, the Apostles from Pentecost, unto Paul, decades later in Rome, this message has been the same.

We are all sinners, deserving death and Hell, but God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son that whosever believeth on Him shall not perish but have everlasting life. That Jesus was Christ, crucified and risen. That by calling upon His name, we are adopted as sons of God, heirs to the promise of the kingdom, and this free gift, given in God's grace can never be lost or taken away.

It is this faith that saves us. Not our works. Not a denomination. Not anything other than believing in your heart this truth of the good news. That once we do, our spirit, dead in sin is quickened by the Holy Spirit, and we are sealed by Him unto the day of judgment, our sins washed clean in Jesus' blood, we are healed by his stripes.

This is the good news. This is the Gospel.
